topics.title: Verbal Aptitude
topics.syllabus: Verbal Aptitude: Basic English grammar (tenses, articles, adjectives, prepositions, conjunctions, verb-noun agreement, and other parts of speech), basic vocabulary (words, idioms, and phrases in context), reading and comprehension, narrative sequencing.

cards.title: The grammar points GATE actually tests
cards.bodyHtml: Five or six patterns account for nearly every grammar question: subject–verb agreement across an intervening phrase, tense consistency, the article before a vowel sound, prepositions fixed by the verb, and misplaced modifiers. Strip a long sentence down to its subject and main verb first — the error is almost always between those two.
cards.pitfallHtml: Collective nouns (team, committee, jury) take a singular verb in Indian/British exam usage. So do each, every, either, neither, none of — regardless of the plural noun that follows.

cards.title: Words and idioms in context
cards.bodyHtml: The word-meaning questions are never asked in isolation — the sentence supplies the sense. Look for the connector: although, despite, whereas signal a contrast so the blank opposes the rest; therefore, since, because signal agreement. Decide the sign of the blank before you look at the options.
cards.pitfallHtml: Idioms are not literal and are not negotiable — let the cat out of the bag, a shot in the arm, on the cards. If you do not know one, do not reason it out word by word; use the sentence's tone instead.

cards.title: Comprehension and narrative sequencing
cards.bodyHtml: Answer only from the passage. For inference questions the right option is the weakest one the passage still supports; options containing always, never, only, all are usually wrong because passages rarely claim that much. For sequencing, find the opening sentence — the one with no pronoun and no back-reference — then chain by pronouns and connectives.

topics.title: Quantitative Aptitude
topics.syllabus: Quantitative Aptitude: Data interpretation - data graphs (bar graphs, pie charts, and other graphs representing data), 2- and 3-dimensional plots, maps, and tables; numerical computation and estimation - ratios, percentages, powers, exponents and logarithms, permutations and combinations, and series; mensuration and geometry; elementary statistics and probability.

cards.title: Permutations, combinations and probability
cards.bodyHtml: Ask one question first: does order matter? If yes it is a permutation, if no a combination. Then ask whether repetition is allowed. Nearly every mistake in this topic is an answer to the wrong one of those two questions.

cards.title: Data interpretation and elementary statistics
cards.bodyHtml: Read the axis units and the footnotes before the numbers — a chart in lakhs against a question in crores is a deliberate trap. For pie charts convert degrees to percentages once (1%=3.6∘1\%=3.6^\circ1%=3.6∘) and reuse it. Estimate first: the options are often far enough apart that a rounded calculation decides the answer.
cards.pitfallHtml: "Percent" and "percentage point" are different. A rise from 20% to 25% is a rise of 5 percentage points but of 25 percent.

topics.title: Analytical Aptitude
topics.syllabus: Analytical Aptitude: Logic - deduction and induction; analogy; numerical relations and reasoning.

cards.title: Deduction, induction and validity
cards.bodyHtml: A conclusion is valid only if it must follow — not if it merely could. Draw the Venn diagram in every way the premises allow; if a single arrangement breaks the conclusion, it does not follow. Real-world truth is irrelevant, which is what makes these questions feel odd.
cards.pitfallHtml: Induction generalises from examples and is never certain; deduction is. If a question asks which conclusion definitely follows, an inductively reasonable option is still the wrong answer.

cards.title: Analogy and numerical relations
cards.bodyHtml: Name the relationship in a short sentence before looking at the options — X is the tool used by Y, X is a part of Y, X is the cause of Y. Then apply that sentence to each option and keep the one that fits exactly, including direction.

cards.title: Arrangements and puzzles
cards.bodyHtml: Start from the most constrained statement, not the first one. Build a grid and enter only what is forced; where two possibilities remain, carry both branches and let a later clue kill one. Guessing early and backtracking wastes more time than carrying two cases.

topics.title: Spatial Aptitude
topics.syllabus: Spatial Aptitude: Transformation of shapes - translation, rotation, scaling, mirroring, assembling, and grouping; paper folding, cutting, and patterns in 2 and 3 dimensions.

cards.title: Rotation, mirroring and scaling
cards.bodyHtml: A rotation preserves handedness; a mirror reverses it. So the fastest test for 'rotated or reflected' is to pick an asymmetric feature and check whether going clockwise around the shape still passes the same features in the same order.

formulas.exprHtml: rotation: order of features preserved; mirror: order reversed\text{rotation: order of features preserved; mirror: order reversed}rotation: order of features preserved; mirror: order reversed

cards.title: Paper folding and cutting
cards.bodyHtml: Work backwards: unfold one crease at a time, and at each unfold mirror every existing hole across that crease line. The number of holes doubles per fold that the cut passes through, so a cut through two folds gives four holes.

cards.bodyHtml: On a cube net, faces two apart in a straight strip are opposite; faces that share an edge or a corner in the net are adjacent. That one rule settles most net questions without any mental rotation.
